before: Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it's okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you've texted "hello??" before they're at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! The texts and the sulking aren't, and the Guide can help you find something that leaves room for both of you, like a hug at the door and a "see you in an hour." But hear your little one out first. I think it just wants to know they're coming back.
after: Forced adulthood can get into your head too, where it wants everything as spotless as that kitchen. At your grandpa's funeral, some dumb jingle starts up in your head and you nearly laugh during the eulogy. That doesn't mean you didn't love him, or that something's wrong with you. Minds come up with ugly and embarrassing stuff all the time, some of it the opposite of what you believe, and bodies do their own thing too. The Guide isn't there to police every thought. It notices the jingle and knows you didn't mean it, and that it isn't who you are. Then it goes with what you'd stand behind, which here is probably squeezing your mom's hand and listening, and lets the jingle go.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Three Adult Functions.
The Guide does not need certainty. It chooses the next sane, value-consistent action while the future remains unknown.

(Queue item, not guide prose; what the public guide is asked to preserve:)
### PGQ-014 — Some real problems are blocked, not actionable yet
Preserve the reader-facing distinction between a concrete problem that has a feasible next action and one whose currently relevant steps are all blocked by a known external prerequisite, permission, timing condition, or unavailable resource. In the blocked state, preserve the actual constraint chain and the condition that would reopen action rather than inventing a workaround that assumes a known constraint away. Waiting for a real external condition is not failed motivation or avoidance; put available effort into another useful priority until the route reopens.

### PGQ-017 — One blocked problem should not block the whole life
Preserve the reader-facing distinction between separate practical lanes. When several real problems coexist, one can be externally blocked while another still has a useful next step. Choose the current practical focus from the person's stated goal, impact, urgency, leverage, and what can actually move now; keep the blocked lane's reopening condition visible without letting it suppress an independent actionable priority. When overwhelm makes everything feel scrambled, reduce the sorting burden: one short organizing statement, one prioritized next step, and only a clarification whose answer would genuinely change that next step. Do not make the person define ordinary words or listen to a long recap when the practical implication is already clear enough.
brief:
- the main point: the Guide doesn't need to know how things will turn out; it picks the next sane step that fits your values, and that's how it keeps the little one growing toward a whole life (the guide's "helps the child grow toward a whole life", whose standards and direction P1 carries).
- the queue items as clauses under that point: a problem can be blocked from outside for now, and waiting on that isn't a lack of motivation or avoidance; no workaround that pretends the block isn't there; keep in view what would reopen it; meanwhile put effort into something else that matters and can move; one stuck problem shouldn't put the whole life on hold.
- context, not for the text: PGQ-017's one short organizing statement and its questions are how a helper talks to someone overwhelmed, so they stay in the AI guide (E156).
